analysis.one_liner: Bans manufacturers from setting minimum prices retailers must charge under antitrust law.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill by voice vote in December 2010, but the full House never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for a manufacturer to agree with a store, wholesaler, or distributor that its product cannot be sold below a set floor price. Such "resale price maintenance" agreements had been automatic violations of the Sherman Antitrust Act for nearly a century until the Supreme Court loosened that rule in 2007, letting courts judge each case individually. The bill would restore the old, stricter rule, making these price-floor agreements illegal across the board so retailers can discount freely.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers gain the most: when stores are free to sell below a manufacturer's floor price, discounts and price competition return, which is why the bill is named the Discount Pricing Consumer Protection Act. Discount retailers, online sellers, and price-cutting stores also gain, because manufacturers can no longer pressure them to charge the same higher price as everyone else. Fans of antitrust enforcement gain a clear rule instead of costly case-by-case litigation.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that any agreement setting a price below which a retailer, wholesaler, or distributor cannot sell a product or service is an illegal restraint of trade under Section 1 of the Sherman Act, restoring the automatic ban courts had applied for decades.
The bill would take effect 90 days after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and brand-name suppliers lose the power to enforce minimum retail prices, which are often used to keep brand image high, protect margins, and prevent stores from discounting. Some small specialty retailers also lose: a price floor can protect them from "free-riding" shoppers who get service and advice at a full-price store but buy at a discounter. The bill's design also imposes antitrust liability without exceptions, which critics of a blanket ban consider overly rigid.

drawbacks.text: The ban is absolute. Courts and many economists have argued that some price-floor agreements are benign, such as protecting small stores from discounters who free-ride on their service; the bill would leave no room for those cases, reclassifying every such agreement as illegal.
The bill was reported with no recorded committee roll call, only voice votes, so there is no record of individual members' positions on it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a real cost to manufacturers and some small service-heavy retailers for lower prices and renewed price competition for consumers. Its main design weakness is that it reinstates a blanket rule with no case-by-case flexibility, which is the same rigidity the Supreme Court rejected in 2007 when it started letting courts evaluate these agreements individually. On balance, the benefit to price-conscious shoppers outweighs that rigidity, but honest supporters should acknowledge the free-riding problem for small stores.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Judiciary Committee on a voice vote and was placed on the House calendar on December 8, 2010, but with just a few weeks left in the Congress, no one ever brought it up for a floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 13, 2009, by Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia, joined by Judiciary Chairman John Conyers, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
It moved quickly at first: a Judiciary subcommittee approved it by voice vote on July 30, 2009, and the full committee ordered it reported by voice vote on January 13, 2010.

The committee formally reported the bill with House Report 111-676 on December 8, 2010, placing it on the Union Calendar, but the House never considered it before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers keep the ability to set minimum retail prices for their products, and consumers never got the discount protections the bill promised. The timing also mattered: the committee reported the bill in the final weeks of the Congress, when a floor vote was unlikely to be scheduled.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Manufacturers that set minimum retail prices

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through subcommittee and committee approval.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.what_they_did: Joined Johnson in introducing the bill and, as committee chairman, brought it through full committee markup and formal report in December 2010.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote after it was placed on the calendar on December 8, 2010.

sides.party_line_note: No recorded roll-call votes were ever taken; the subcommittee and committee approved it by voice vote, and the only identifiable supporters, the sponsor and three cosponsors, were all Democrats.

industries.industry: Brand-name manufacturers and consumer product suppliers
industries.note: The bill strips these companies of the power to set minimum retail prices, a tool used to protect brand image and keep margins high. Their interest in keeping that power runs against shoppers who want lower prices.

Stores that compete on price would be free to sell below manufacturer floor prices without fear of losing the supplier's business. Their interest in discounting matches shoppers' interest in low prices.

Many of these stores have been able to hold prices up through manufacturer price floors, which shielded them from discounters' price cutting. A blanket ban removes that protection, and economists debate whether those floors help or hurt them in the long run.
